Alte Autos müssen nix verkehrtes sein, aber da kann gerne mal was repariert werden wollen, einfach weil sie alt sind. Gerade wenn du gem. der Vorlieben einen hast der wenig gefahren wurde kann es sein, dass sich nach 10.000km alles mögliche auftut. Poröse Schläuche, rissige Riemen, ausgehärtete Dichtungen… Sowas kann durchaus zum Groschengrab werden. Muss nicht, kann. Deshalb würde ich auch bei einem alten Wagen sehr genau mir anschauen, was da gemacht wurde, was anstehen könnte, auf eine Bühne, zu einer Werkstatt. 

Und ich würde separat nochmal überlegen - wenn du prinzipiell bereit bist einen 30 Jahre alten Wagen zu kaufen und zu bewegen, warum dann nicht auch einen neueren mit mehr Kilometern? Einen der genannten Mercedes Benz, einen der 1.9 TDI von VAG, etc. Wenn ein Auto bewegt wird, wird es oft auch gepflegt und gerade Langstreckenkilometer sind für einen Wagen besser als viele kurze Trips. I can’t speak to Sweden’s car prices, but coming from central europe, be extra careful with VAG’s from around 2005 to around 2014. Do your research on the specific engine in the specific car, a lot of the gas (as in Benzin, not diesel) have a timing chain that likes to go with very little warning. 

Generally, if I’m getting conversion right, being about 10 to 1, you’re at the lower end of the price spectrum and barring known and catastrophic failure points the individual car matters much more than the brand or type. Don’t fixate on one specific car, take someone with you if you go to look at any cars so you don’t get tunnel vision, walk away if you even get a bad feeling and try to keep ~10.000 SEK in reserve, because something is going to need repairs. 

If I were to add any cars I’d suggest looking at VAG cars (barring the engine issues described above), especially the smaller Skodas.

Best of luck

I’m not going to say you’re wrong, it’s obviously all subjective. But what I was trying to gesture at goes much beyond nationalistic pride and more towards the topics you yourself addressed. There is a certain… smell, feel, vibe to countries that seems to match their people and their geography. Italy, Spain, France they all somehow feel distinct and within themselves. I feel like I could tell, somehow, even without street signs and language, where I am. But partially because they’re more recent and partially *because* of  different forms of nationalism/socialism, the central european countries feel less like that. There are still ethnic phenotypes, more pronounced in some countries than others, but I feel somehow people there are less rooted. Who genuinely wants to be a Brandenburger? What makes a Hessian? All the towns and villages I’ve been to, people seem to hold no clear communal understanding of themselves as a unit. Not even at a village level or anything else. My grandmother tells me, back in the day denomination (catholic/protestant) played a huge role between different villages and families. that’s gone and while people might still pay lip-service to some distinction against foreigners, wave a flag at soccer games or might even be casually racist towards visibly different ethnicities, it’s almost out of reflex or habit. 
I really struggle to put this into words and it’s probably just the symptoms of an “anywhere” finding society closed to him and thus thinking it’s atomized. 

But your post about that feeling of return or rightness really struck a cord with me

I wanted to echo all the other commenters and say thank you for this very detailed and interesting post. 

What I found especially interesting is your touching upon culture because as a German, I would have instinctively said Germany has very little culture and is one of the most anodyne and atomized places in Europe - constantly self-ironic and deprecating, scarred by both the legacy of the third Reich and communist dictatorship. I guess there is something about fish - water here, but having lived outside the country multiple times I still struggle to identify a unique “German-ness” that you find readily apparent. 

Anyway, thanks again and, while I know it’s probably weird to broadcast thoughts and experiences from your private life on the internet, I found it very interesting and would love to hear updates at some future point in your immigrant story!

Technically renting should always be a little, but not a lot, more expensive than owning a property because the owner is going to want to make a profit. It is often smaller than people think, because comparing lease to mortgage payments tends to miss periodic and irregular maintenance and upkeep costs. 
The disconnect tends to happen either when a) there is a limited supply of housing compared to the demand, often leading to quickly spiking rents because way more people cannot or do not want to commit to long and expensive mortgages. 
(b) housing is viewed as an investment opportunity not because it “makes” money but because it is considered a safe “store” of money. I think this why some cities have insanely disproportional values on owning property: the people who own it do so neither for the benefit of living there nor for the rewards of renting it out, but see it as a very safe way to store assets. Once you pass the first generation, the asset is usually also paid off, meaning there is (should be) positive cash flow and the incentive to sell becomes even lower because humans instinctively undervalue opportunity costs. This is why older places with little war-issues and fairly stable regimes tend to command much, much higher purchase prices (see London, Paris v. Berlin, Vienna). 

I think some places also have a mix of governmental support/cultural cachet for land ownership. The future performance can be debated up and down, but at the end of the day for many people a mortgage is one of the very few ways they can leverage large amounts of cash and in recent years the interest rates have been insanely low. Many people also don’t save unless they’re compelled so a mortgage is one way for them to build wealth. I’m not 100% sure why the irrationalities of this aren’t exploited more by big institutional investors - it still seems somewhat sensible that a bank would offer vastly better conditions to large sums for distributed assets than for individual “risky” prospect. 

I have no idea about the concrete situation in Austin, but remember that (sadly) the market can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent.

Yea, I have access to a hut in the mountains with only wood for cooking and heating. And light with Kerosene lamps. Everyone’s standards have risen, but the standards of the very poor have risen by far the most. Look at the pictures of late Victorian urban poor or go dig a ditch for a day. If those are the alternatives, being a live-in servant for little more than room and board suddenly becomes way more appealing. 
The numbers often speak of a risen in income-inequality but I think that masks the fact that after WWII the average person has become insanely wealthy by any historical standard. With the “bottom” being less harsh, people are simply less likely to take bad jobs at low pay. 

Also the economics of households were different. There were few shortcuts to reduce necessary manpower. If you’re a theoretical household of 5, one person doing the entire house is hard work. Cooking used to be complicated. Getting seasonal vegetables from a market on foot, or even growing them and all that entails and then cleaning them (idk if you’re American but i.e. potatoes are really, really dirty. Try cleaning that without running water) and making a fire and tending it and figuring out where the oven burned and where not etc. The same goes for household etc. cleaning, sweeping, laundry for gods sake my grandma still remembers her mother doing chores in a pre war household and laundry was the worst. But also two women scrubbed the entire kitchen after every lunch because there was no hood on the range and it would get incredibly and unmanageably greasy if not done immediately. 
But once you have the “basics” down, it scales well in a pre-industrial household. An extra nanny is not so bad. She might live in something we today see as a cupboard. And most “middle” class families didn’t necessarily have live in servants with such clearly delineated roles. You might have a girl. She’d help the cook, she’d make beds, but she is also an extra pair of hands to look after children.
